FIRST WARN FORECAST
Tuesday, September 8, 2026

First. Accurate. Trusted.

HEAT RETURNS TODAY, STORMS RETURN WEDNESDAY

After a brief break from the heat on Labor Day, summer returns today with temperatures climbing back into the 90s. A Heat Advisory is in effect for portions of central Missouri, where a combination of higher humidity and temperatures in the mid to upper 90s will produce heat index values around 105 degrees for several hours this afternoon. Elsewhere, humidity will remain somewhat lower, keeping heat index values closer to actual air temperatures.

The heat will be short-lived. A cold front will approach the region Wednesday, bringing increasing humidity, a growing chance for showers and thunderstorms, and eventually much cooler temperatures. The timing of that front will be critical to Wednesday's forecast. Depending on how quickly it moves south, temperatures could range from the low to upper 90s before storms and clouds become more widespread.

Today, an unusually strong upper-level ridge will become centered over the Mid-Mississippi River Valley, producing abundant sunshine and another day of well-above-average temperatures. Afternoon highs should reach the low to mid-90s across most of the area, with mid to upper 90s more likely across central Missouri. Dewpoints will remain mainly in the upper 50s and 60s, limiting the heat index for much of the region. Central Missouri will be the exception, where dewpoints approaching 70 degrees combined with warmer temperatures will create several hours of heat index values near 105 degrees.

Tonight will remain mild, with increasing clouds and humidity ahead of Wednesday's approaching front. Temperatures will generally fall into the upper 60s and 70s.

Wednesday will bring a much more complicated weather setup. A cold front associated with a deepening storm system over Canada will move southward into the Mid-Mississippi River Valley. Current guidance increasingly favors the front reaching the I-70 corridor around midday, although there remains some uncertainty regarding exactly how quickly it will progress.

Showers and thunderstorms could already be occurring Wednesday morning, primarily behind the front. A relative decrease in storm coverage may occur around midday and into the afternoon before activity increases again later Wednesday as stronger upper-level forcing arrives. South of the front, temperatures could still climb into the 90s, but increasing clouds and the timing of the front make the high-temperature forecast uncertain.

Humidity will increase substantially Wednesday, with moisture pooling along and ahead of the front. That raises the possibility of heat index values reaching 105 degrees or higher, but it remains unclear whether temperatures will remain high enough long enough for that threshold to be reached. For that reason, an additional Heat Advisory has not been issued at this time, although it remains a possibility depending on how the forecast evolves.

The more significant weather concern Wednesday will be the increasing potential for showers and thunderstorms. Storm coverage should increase Wednesday evening as a stronger upper-level disturbance approaches and atmospheric lift increases. By Wednesday night into Thursday morning, showers and thunderstorms are expected to become widespread across much of the region.

While a few strong storms are possible, the overall severe weather threat remains somewhat uncertain. A layer of warm air aloft may suppress storms in the warm sector, while the strongest wind shear and upper-level forcing could remain behind the surface cold front. This setup may favor the strongest and most organized storms occurring north of the front rather than as surface-based severe thunderstorms. Gusty winds and small hail will be the primary concerns, although locally stronger storms cannot be ruled out.

Heavy rainfall is another concern Wednesday night into Thursday morning. The atmosphere will contain an unusually large amount of moisture, with precipitable water values exceeding two inches. The slow movement of the front and thunderstorms developing along it could allow some areas to receive several rounds of rainfall.

Most locations are currently expected to receive roughly one-quarter inch to one inch of rain through Thursday, with a corridor of potentially higher totals between one and three inches possible somewhere near the I-44 and I-70 corridors. The good news is that soils across the region remain quite dry following the recent heat and lack of rainfall. That means much of this rain would be beneficial, and the risk of widespread flash flooding is currently limited despite the potential for locally heavy rainfall.

Showers and a few thunderstorms could linger into Thursday before the upper-level disturbance pushes the front and remaining precipitation farther south. Areas along and south of the I-44 and I-70 corridors could remain cloudy and wet for much of Thursday, with temperatures struggling to rise above 80 degrees. Areas farther north should see clouds gradually decrease and temperatures reach the low 80s.

Beyond Thursday, the weather pattern becomes more progressive and somewhat unsettled. A frontal boundary is expected to linger somewhere across the broader Mid-Mississippi River Valley, with additional waves of clouds, showers and thunderstorms possible from Friday night into the weekend. However, the forecast does not currently suggest continuous rainfall. Ensemble guidance continues to show more dry periods than wet periods through early next week.

Temperatures during the latter part of the week should be considerably cooler than what we experience today and Wednesday, although still somewhat above average for September. Current guidance favors afternoon highs generally in the low 80s to low 90s, depending on cloud cover, rainfall and the eventual position of the frontal boundary.

The bottom line is that the heat returns today, but it will not last. A Heat Advisory is in effect for portions of central Missouri, where heat index values around 105 degrees are expected this afternoon. Wednesday will bring increasing humidity and another hot day for some areas, but the approaching cold front introduces considerable uncertainty regarding temperatures and whether another heat headline will be necessary.

The bigger story Wednesday into Thursday will be the return of widespread showers and thunderstorms. Gusty winds, small hail and locally heavy rainfall will be possible, with the potential for one to three inches of rain in a corridor near I-44 and I-70. Most of that rainfall should be beneficial given the very dry conditions across the region.

After Thursday, temperatures settle into a much more manageable range, with additional chances for showers and thunderstorms as the frontal boundary lingers nearby. The prolonged summer heatwave is behind us. While more warmth is likely, the pattern ahead looks much more like September than the relentless heat we experienced last week.
severeNarrative:
First Warn Forecast & Severe Weather Outlook Update
11:50 AM CDT | Wednesday, June 17, 2026
First Warn Weather Alert Day
Headlines
Severe thunderstorms remain likely this afternoon and evening across Missouri and Illinois.
Damaging winds up to 85 mph, large hail up to 2.5 inches, and several tornadoes remain possible.
The greatest threat locally remains across eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois, including the St. Louis metro area.
Strong southwest winds will gust between 40 and 50 mph outside of thunderstorms.
Peak severe weather threat for the St. Louis area remains between 6 PM and 9 PM.

A potentially dangerous severe weather outbreak remains on track across portions of Missouri and Illinois this afternoon and evening. There has been little change in the overall forecast since this morning. The Storm Prediction Center continues to highlight much of eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois in an Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5) for severe weather, while portions of central Illinois remain under a Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5) where the highest threat for significant severe weather exists.

An intense cluster of thunderstorms that developed overnight across Iowa produced wind gusts exceeding 90 mph and continues to influence the forecast across Illinois late this morning. The primary outflow boundary currently extends from far northeast Missouri into portions of south-central Illinois. This boundary will likely serve as a focus for severe thunderstorm development later today.

Strong sunshine south of the boundary is allowing temperatures to rapidly climb through the 80s while dew points remain in the upper 60s and lower 70s. Combined with an exceptionally strong wind field aloft, conditions remain favorable for supercells capable of producing all severe weather hazards.

While morning storms may slightly alter where the greatest risk ultimately develops, confidence remains high that numerous severe thunderstorms will develop this afternoon and continue through the evening hours.

Primary Threats

🌪 Several Tornadoes Possible

A few strong tornadoes remain possible.
Greatest tornado threat remains across central Illinois.
Tornadoes remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois, especially near any lingering outflow boundaries.

💨 Destructive Winds Possible

Widespread damaging winds of 60 to 80 mph.
Isolated wind gusts exceeding 85 mph remain possible.
Significant tree damage and widespread power outages could occur.

🧊 Large to Very Large Hail

Large hail remains possible with discrete supercells.
Hailstones up to 2.5 inches in diameter may occur.
Timing Across Missouri and Illinois
1 PM - 3 PM

The first severe thunderstorms are expected to develop across northeast Missouri and portions of west-central Illinois. Areas near Quincy, Kirksville, Palmyra, Hannibal, and surrounding communities should closely monitor conditions.

3 PM - 6 PM

The severe weather threat expands southeast into central Missouri and western Illinois. Columbia, Jefferson City, Mexico, Bowling Green, Troy, and portions of the northern St. Louis metro could see supercells capable of producing tornadoes, very large hail, and destructive winds.

6 PM - 9 PM

This remains the peak severe weather window for the St. Louis metropolitan area and much of eastern Missouri and western Illinois. Storms may become more widespread during this period while maintaining the potential to produce damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes. Residents from St. Louis and St. Charles to Edwardsville, Belleville, Alton, Farmington, and surrounding communities should be prepared to act quickly if warnings are issued.

9 PM - Midnight

Storms are expected to organize into a line extending from central Missouri into southern Indiana. Damaging straight-line winds become the primary threat as storms shift into southeast Missouri and southern Illinois. Heavy rainfall and localized flooding may also develop overnight.

Local First Warn Outlook

The highest confidence for severe weather today exists across the Enhanced Risk area covering much of eastern and central Missouri, including Columbia, Jefferson City, the St. Louis metro, northeast Missouri, and west-central Illinois.

Farther south, a Slight Risk extends across southern Missouri and southern Illinois, including Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon. Severe thunderstorms remain possible in these areas, but storm coverage and intensity may be somewhat lower than locations farther north.

The lowest severe weather threat remains across the Missouri Bootheel and far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border where a Marginal Risk remains in place. However, isolated severe storms cannot be ruled out.

Threat Levels

🔴 Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5)

Central Illinois
Areas northeast of Springfield, Illinois
Greatest potential for strong tornadoes and destructive winds

🟤 Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5)

Northeast Missouri
Central Missouri
Eastern Missouri
St. Louis Metro
West-central Illinois
Southwest Illinois

🟡 Slight Risk (Level 2 of 5)

Southern Missouri
South-central Missouri
Southeast Missouri
Southern Illinois
Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon

🟢 Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 5)

Missouri Bootheel
Far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border
Areas south of Poplar Bluff and near Paducah
Additional Concern: Strong Winds Outside of Storms

Even outside of thunderstorms, strong southwest winds will continue through the afternoon. Sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts of 40 to 50 mph are expected. Loose outdoor objects should be secured, and travel may become difficult for high-profile vehicles.

Thursday Outlook

The cold front responsible for today's severe weather will gradually move south of the region overnight. Showers and a few thunderstorms may linger into Thursday, especially across southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois. Cooler temperatures in the 70s and lower 80s will provide a welcome break from today's heat and humidity.

Bottom Line

There has been little change in the forecast thinking since this morning. The atmosphere remains primed for severe thunderstorm development this afternoon and evening. While the greatest threat for strong tornadoes remains across central Illinois, all severe weather hazards remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois.

The St. Louis metro remains in the corridor for severe weather between 6 PM and 9 PM, with damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes all possible. Everyone across the First Warn viewing area should remain weather aware and have multiple ways to receive warnings throughout the day and tonight.

First Warn Weather: First. Accurate. Trusted.
